<reason>Side B (PRO) won a closely fought, high-quality exchange. B's decisive move was the reciprocity reframe: compulsory schooling means every native child is legally required to clear the language/civics bar, so expecting adult newcomers to acquire the same content is "same bar, different delivery," not a second constitution. A's pressure questions were excellent — Q1 (what observable test proves adoption?) and Q2 (name a native failure that makes membership incomplete) exposed real burdens — and B answered both directly with plausible content (measurable language tests, conduct-based indicators, front-loaded childhood requirements). A's best surviving point is that adult natives who skip everything keep the franchise, making the immigrant demand origin-based; B blunted this with the "practically crippled / state failure / front-loaded delivery" response, though not fully. B's notable flaws: B4.5 misdescribes A's answer as "went unanswered" when A had listed proactive inspectors, hotlines, and shelters, and two B turns were clipped. A was rhetorically sharper ("second childhood assigned by birthplace," "conscript a kitchen," "membership as performance review") and answered B's pressure honestly, but the closing mostly restated the asymmetry rather than resolving B's schooling concession, which B exploited effectively in its own closing. Net: B made the debate easier to decide on the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Q2 ("name one norm failure that makes a native-born adult incomplete") forced B to concede no adult native is ever re-tested, producing A's sharpest line — "a native's skip is eccentricity; an immigrant's skip is unfinished membership." B's counter, that compulsory schooling is the universally applied bar and adult immigrants merely missed the childhood delivery, was the exchange that ultimately decided the debate, crystallized in B's closing: "extra measured against what? A bar every native child is legally required to clear."</best_rebuttal>
